claim: Blood samples were collected from two healthy donors (M1 male age 26, and P30 male age 39) on multiple timepoints before and after immunization with YFV17D vaccine.
source: Blood samples were collected from two healthy donors (M1 male age 26, and P30 male age 39) on multiple timepoints before and after immunization with YFV17D vaccine.
evidence: Direct statement in the Materials and methods section describing the study participants and sample collection.

claim: The study was approved by the institutional review board (IRB) of Pirogov Russian National Research Medical University.
source: The study was approved by the institutional review board (IRB) of Pirogov Russian National Research Medical University.
evidence: Direct statement about ethical approval in the Materials and methods section.

claim: 1580 TCR beta and 1566 TCR alpha clonotypes were significantly expanded after primary immunization.
source: Overall we found 1580 TCR beta and 1566 TCR alpha clonotypes significantly expanded after the primary immunization, respectively occupying 6.7% and 7.8% of the sampled TCR repertoire of bulk PBMCs in cumulative frequency at the peak of the response (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: Quantitative results from TCR repertoire sequencing analysis presented in text and Figure 1B,C.

claim: YF-responding clonotypes occupied 6.7% (TCR beta) and 7.8% (TCR alpha) of the sampled TCR repertoire of bulk PBMCs in cumulative frequency at the peak of the primary response.
source: Overall we found 1580 TCR beta and 1566 TCR alpha clonotypes significantly expanded after the primary immunization, respectively occupying 6.7% and 7.8% of the sampled TCR repertoire of bulk PBMCs in cumulative frequency at the peak of the response (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from TCR sequencing data reported in text and shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: During the primary response, T-cells expanded intensely with a cumulative increase of about 950-fold within 2–3 weeks after YF immunization.
source: In accordance with previous studies (Miller et al., 2008; Blom et al., 2013; Akondy et al., 2009; Kongsgaard et al., 2017; Pogorelyy et al., 2018), we show that during the primary response T-cells expanded intensely (with cumulative increase of about 950-fold) within 2–3 weeks after YF immunization.
evidence: Quantitative measurement from TCR sequencing data, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The cumulative frequency of YF-responding clonotypes increased ≈2.5-fold at the peak of the response after the second immunization, reaching 0.5% of the TCR repertoire.
source: The cumulative frequency of these clonotypes increased ≈2.5-fold at the peak of the response after the second immunization, reaching 0.5% of the TCR repertoire (Figure 1D, blue curve).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from TCR sequencing data after booster vaccination, shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The secondary response was weaker but happened much faster than the primary one, with a peak frequency of responding clonotypes occurring on day 5 instead of day 15 after vaccination.
source: The secondary response was weaker, but happened much faster than the primary one, with a peak frequency of responding clonotypes occurring on day 5 instead of day 15 after vaccination.
evidence: Comparison of temporal dynamics between primary and secondary responses from TCR sequencing data.

claim: 73 additional responding clonotypes were identified in the secondary response, but their impact on the magnitude of the secondary response was negligible.
source: Although we identified 73 additional responding clonotypes, their impact on the magnitude of the secondary response was negligible and we did not use them for further analyses (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Quantitative result from edgeR analysis of secondary immunization timepoints, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: No substantial recruitment of naive clones was found in the response to the booster vaccination.
source: In summary, we found no evidence of substantial recruitment of naive clones in the response to the booster vaccination.
evidence: Conclusion based on analysis of clonotypes identified in secondary response.

claim: After booster immunization in donor M1, YF-responding CD4+ cells peaked earlier (day 5 vs day 10) than CD8+ T-cells.
source: After booster immunization in donor M1, YF-responding CD4+ cells peaked earlier (day 5 vs day 10) and expanded much more (≈8 times vs. ≈1.5 times) than CD8+ T-cells (Figure 1D, green and pink curves).
evidence: Temporal analysis of CD4+ and CD8+ subsets from TCR sequencing data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: After booster immunization in donor M1, YF-responding CD4+ cells expanded much more (≈8 times vs. ≈1.5 times) than CD8+ T-cells.
source: After booster immunization in donor M1, YF-responding CD4+ cells peaked earlier (day 5 vs day 10) and expanded much more (≈8 times vs. ≈1.5 times) than CD8+ T-cells (Figure 1D, green and pink curves).
evidence: Quantitative comparison of expansion magnitudes between CD4+ and CD8+ subsets from TCR sequencing data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: During primary immunization, both CD4+ and CD8+ subsets peaked on day 15.
source: During primary immunization, the difference in response dynamics between CD4+ and CD8+ subsets was less prominent, as they both peaked on day 15.
evidence: Temporal analysis of CD4+ and CD8+ subset dynamics during primary response.

claim: By day 21 after primary immunization, CD4+ responding clones contracted much more (to 43.6% of peak frequency) than CD8+ clonotypes (87% of peak frequency).
source: However, by day 21 CD4+ responding clones contracted much more (to 43.6% of peak frequency) than CD8+ clonotypes (87% of peak frequency).
evidence: Quantitative measurement of contraction rates for CD4+ and CD8+ subsets from TCR sequencing data.

claim: The CD4 response precedes the CD8 response.
source: These observations confirm previous reports that the CD4 response precedes the CD8 response (Blom et al., 2013).
evidence: Conclusion based on temporal dynamics analysis, supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Donor P30 received the first YF-vaccine 30 years earlier and has not been in YF endemic areas for at least 28 years.
source: To see how long-lived T-cell memory response to YF can be, we recruited an additional donor (P30), who received the first YF-vaccine 30 years earlier and has not been in YF endemic areas for at least 28 years.
evidence: Description of donor P30's vaccination history in the Results section.

claim: Donor P30 had 204 TCR beta and 201 TCR alpha responding clonotypes after booster vaccination.
source: Both the numbers of responding clonotypes (204 for TCR beta and 201 for TCR alpha) and the maximum frequency at the peak of the response (0.69%) were much lower than for any primary vaccinee both from this and other studies (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Quantitative results from TCR sequencing analysis of donor P30, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The maximum frequency of responding clonotypes at the peak of the response in donor P30 was 0.69%.
source: Both the numbers of responding clonotypes (204 for TCR beta and 201 for TCR alpha) and the maximum frequency at the peak of the response (0.69%) were much lower than for any primary vaccinee both from this and other studies (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from TCR sequencing data of donor P30, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The numbers of responding clonotypes and maximum frequency at peak response in donor P30 were much lower than for any primary vaccinee.
source: Both the numbers of responding clonotypes (204 for TCR beta and 201 for TCR alpha) and the maximum frequency at the peak of the response (0.69%) were much lower than for any primary vaccinee both from this and other studies (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Comparative analysis between donor P30 and primary vaccinees, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The response to booster vaccination in donor P30 was characterized by a large expansion between days 0 and 5, and a peak on day 10, for both CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells.
source: The response to the booster vaccination was characterized by a large expansion between days 0 and 5, and a peak on day 10, for both CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells.
evidence: Temporal analysis of CD4+ and CD8+ subset dynamics in donor P30 from TCR sequencing data.

claim: The dynamics and magnitude of the response to booster vaccination in donor P30 was very similar to the response to booster vaccination after 18 months in donor M1.
source: Overall the dynamics and the magnitude of this response was very similar to the response to the booster vaccination after 18 months we observed in donor M1 (Figure 1C), suggesting that protection against the virus was maintained even after 30 years.
evidence: Comparative analysis between donor P30 and donor M1 booster responses, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Protection against the yellow fever virus was maintained even after 30 years.
source: Overall the dynamics and the magnitude of this response was very similar to the response to the booster vaccination after 18 months we observed in donor M1 (Figure 1C), suggesting that protection against the virus was maintained even after 30 years.
evidence: Inference based on similarity of booster responses between donors M1 and P30, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The overall response strength to secondary immunization was an order of magnitude lower compared to the primary response.
source: We already showed that the overall response strength to secondary immunization was an order of magnitude lower compared to the primary response.
evidence: Quantitative comparison between primary and secondary responses from TCR sequencing data.

claim: Several clones showed remarkable expansion rates and peak frequencies upon secondary immunization, comparable to those observed in primary immunization.
source: However, several clones showed remarkable expansion rates and peak frequencies, comparable to the ones observed in primary immunization.
evidence: Analysis of individual clonal trajectories from TCR sequencing data.

claim: Clones with high expansion rates upon secondary immunization were observed in both donors upon secondary immunization after 18 months and 30 years.
source: Such clones were observed in both donors upon secondary immunization after 18 months and 30 years (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Analysis of individual clonal trajectories shown in Figure 2A, 2B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Akondy et al. using deuterium labeling showed a half-life of 123 days for cells specific to the immunodominant epitope NS4B214-222.
source: Previously, Akondy et al. using deuterium labeling of cells specific to the immunodominant epitope NS4B214-222 (as determined by a A02-NS4B214-222-multimer binding assay) showed a very similar half-life of 123 days (Akondy et al., 2017).
evidence: Citation to previous study by Akondy et al., 2017.

claim: 96% of CD4+ clones that responded to primary immunization could be re-identified in at least one sample after booster immunization.
source: By contrast, in our sample we could re-identify 96% of CD4+ and 88% of CD8+ clones that responded to the primary immunization in at least one sample after the booster immunization.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of clonotype persistence from TCR sequencing data.

claim: 88% of CD8+ clones that responded to primary immunization could be re-identified in at least one sample after booster immunization.
source: By contrast, in our sample we could re-identify 96% of CD4+ and 88% of CD8+ clones that responded to the primary immunization in at least one sample after the booster immunization.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of clonotype persistence from TCR sequencing data.

claim: Practically all the diversity of the responding repertoire is maintained in memory.
source: This suggests that practically all the diversity of the responding repertoire is maintained in memory.
evidence: Inference based on high percentage of re-identified clonotypes after booster immunization.

claim: DeWitt et al. reported that only 5–6% of YF-responding clones are preserved as immune memory, with preferential recruitment of large clones.
source: It was previously reported that only 5–6% of YF-responding clones are preserved as immune memory, with the preferential recruitment of large clones (DeWitt et al., 2015).
evidence: Citation to previous study by DeWitt et al., 2015.

claim: The larger fraction of re-identified YF-responding clones in comparison to previous work may be explained by the sampling depth.
source: The larger fraction of re-identified YF-responding clones in comparison to previous work may be explained by the sampling depth.
evidence: Speculation about methodological differences explaining discrepancy with previous study.

claim: The largest YF-specific CD8+ clones did not expand in response to the booster vaccine.
source: Interestingly, we found that the largest YF-specific CD8+ clones did not expand in response to the booster vaccine.
evidence: Analysis of clonotype expansion patterns shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The most expanded CD8+ clonotypes after booster immunization were rare prior to the booster immunization.
source: Instead, the most expanded clonotypes were rare prior to the booster immunization (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Analysis of clonotype frequencies before and after booster shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Both high and low-frequency CD4+ clones expanded in response to the booster immunization.
source: The situation was different for CD4+ cells: both high and low-frequency CD4+ clones expanded in response to the booster immunization (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Analysis of CD4+ clonotype expansion patterns shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The specific features of clonal trajectories shared by YF-responding clones make it possible to distinguish them from non-expanding clones using unsupervised clustering.
source: The specific features of clonal trajectories shared by YF-responding clones make it possible to distinguish them from non-expanding clones, using unsupervised clustering (see Figure 2—figure supplement 4AB and Materials and methods).
evidence: Demonstration of clustering method shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4AB.

claim: The unsupervised clustering method for identifying YF-responding clones shows good concordance with edgeR and works also without biological replicates.
source: This method shows good concordance with edgeR and works also without biological replicates.
evidence: Comparison of clustering method with edgeR results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4AB.

claim: The heterogeneity of clonal trajectories can be leveraged to computationally pair alpha and beta chains from bulk alpha and beta sequencing data.
source: In addition, we demonstrated that the heterogeneity of clonal trajectories could be leveraged to computationally pair alpha and beta chains from from bulk alpha and beta sequencing data, by exploiting the similarity of trajectories of alpha and beta clonotypes belonging to the same clone (see Figure 2—figure supplement 4C and Materials and methods).
evidence: Demonstration of computational pairing method shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4C.

claim: Several studies have reported subsets of long-lived memory YF-specific T-cells, whose concentration remained stable for years.
source: Several studies have reported subsets of long-lived memory YF-specific T-cells, whose concentration remained stable for years (Fuertes Marraco et al., 2015; Akondy et al., 2017).
evidence: Citations to previous studies by Fuertes Marraco et al., 2015 and Akondy et al., 2017.

claim: Long-lived memory cells are the progenies of effector cells, which divide vigorously during the peak of the response to the vaccine.
source: It was shown that these long-lived memory cells are the progenies of effector cells, which divide vigorously during the peak of the response to the vaccine (Akondy et al., 2017).
evidence: Citation to previous study by Akondy et al., 2017.

claim: TCR sequences can be used as 'barcodes' to measure transitions between different memory subsets after YF immunization.
source: TCR sequences can be used as 'barcodes' to measure transitions between different memory subsets after YF immunization, defined by their surface markers revealed by flow cytometry.
evidence: Description of methodological approach for tracking memory subset transitions.

claim: Three conventional T-cell memory subpopulations were isolated: effector memory (EM, CCR7-CD45RA-), effector memory re-expressing CD45RA (EMRA, CCR7-CD45RA+), and central memory (CM, CCR7+CD45RA-).
source: We isolated with FACS (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for the gating strategy) and sequenced TCR repertoires of 3 conventional T-cell memory subpopulations (Fuertes Marraco et al., 2015; Appay et al., 2008): effector memory (EM, CCR7-CD45RA-), effector memory re-expressing CD45RA (EMRA, CCR7-CD45RA+), and central memory (CM, CCR7+CD45RA-) on days 0, 15, 45, and 18 months after the primary vaccination of donor M1 and on days 0, 15, and 45 after the second vaccination of donor P30.
evidence: Description of experimental methods with citations to previous studies defining these subsets.

claim: On day 45, Tscm (T-cell stem cell-like memory) subset (CCR7+CD45RA+CD95+) was also isolated and sequenced.
source: On day 45 we also isolated and sequenced the repertoire of the recently described Tscm (T-cell stem cell-like memory) subset (CCR7+CD45RA+CD95+).
evidence: Description of experimental methods for Tscm subset isolation.

claim: The memory status of T-cell clones was tightly correlated with their CD4/CD8 status.
source: In agreement with previous studies the memory status of T-cell clones was tightly correlated with their CD4/CD8 status (Sathaliyawala et al., 2013; Thome et al., 2014).
evidence: Analysis of memory subset distribution with citations to previous studies.

claim: The vast majority of CD4+ T-cells were distributed between EM and CM, with <1% in EMRA.
source: The vast majority of CD4+ T-cells were distributed between EM and CM, with <1% in EMRA, while CD8+ T-cell clones were predominantly found in EM and EMRA with ∼2% in CM.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of memory subset distribution from TCR sequencing data.

claim: CD8+ T-cell clones were predominantly found in EM and EMRA with ∼2% in CM.
source: The vast majority of CD4+ T-cells were distributed between EM and CM, with <1% in EMRA, while CD8+ T-cell clones were predominantly found in EM and EMRA with ∼2% in CM.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of memory subset distribution from TCR sequencing data.

claim: For most CD8+ clonotypes in the total repertoire, EM/EMRA phenotypes were stable between day 15 and day 45.
source: While for most CD8+ clonotypes in the total repertoire EM/EMRA phenotypes were stable between day 15 and day 45 (Figure 3B, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,C), the distribution of CD8+ YF-responding clones between memory subsets was significantly shifted towards the EMRA phenotype (Figure 3C).
evidence: Analysis of memory phenotype stability shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,C.

claim: The distribution of CD8+ YF-responding clones between memory subsets was significantly shifted towards the EMRA phenotype.
source: While for most CD8+ clonotypes in the total repertoire EM/EMRA phenotypes were stable between day 15 and day 45 (Figure 3B, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,C), the distribution of CD8+ YF-responding clones between memory subsets was significantly shifted towards the EMRA phenotype (Figure 3C).
evidence: Statistical analysis of memory subset distribution shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The shift towards EMRA phenotype in CD8+ YF-responding clones results from two processes: the rapid decay of EM cells and the phenotype switch from EM to EMRA.
source: This shift results from two processes: the rapid decay of EM cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B) and the phenotype switch from EM to EMRA (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Analysis of memory subset transitions shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and 2D.

claim: Almost all YF-responding CD8+ clones detected 18 months after the first immunization corresponded to the EMRA phenotype.
source: Almost all YF-responding CD8+ clones detected 18 months after the first immunization corresponded to the EMRA phenotype (among 71 clones found in more than three copies in bulk repertoire at day 0 before second vaccination, 41 were found only in the EMRA subset, four only in EM, and six in both).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of memory subset distribution 18 months after primary immunization.

claim: No trend in phenotype switching between days 15 and 45 after vaccination was observed for CD4+ T-cells.
source: For CD4+ T-cells, we did not observe any trend in phenotype switching between days 15 and 45 after the vaccination.
evidence: Analysis of CD4+ memory subset transitions from TCR sequencing data.

claim: Switching from EM to CM phenotype in CD4+ cells was masked due to homing of CM cells to lymphoid organs, defined by the expression of the CCR7 chemokine receptor.
source: We hypothesize that switching from EM to CM phenotype was masked due to homing of CM cells to lymphoid organs, defined by the expression of the CCR7 chemokine receptor.
evidence: Hypothesis proposed to explain lack of observed phenotype switching in CD4+ cells.

claim: In HLA-A02 donors, the NS4B214-222 LLWNGPMAV immunodominant epitope elicits the strongest CD8+ T-cell response.
source: It was previously shown that in HLA-A02 donors the NS4B214-222 LLWNGPMAV immunodominant epitope elicits the strongest CD8+ T-cell response (Akondy et al., 2009; Wieten et al., 2016; Kongsgaard et al., 2017; Blom et al., 2013).
evidence: Citations to multiple previous studies demonstrating immunodominance of NS4B epitope.

claim: Approximately 2100 alpha and 2000 beta functional receptor chains were obtained from NS4B-specific CD8+ T-cells.
source: We obtained ≈2100 alpha and ≈2000 beta functional receptor chains, one of the largest datasets for TCRs with a single specificity.
evidence: Quantitative description of TCR sequencing data from NS4B-specific cells.

claim: At the peak of the response, approximately 24% of all YF-responding CD8+ T-cells were specific to NS4B in donor P30.
source: At the peak of the response, approximately 24% of all YF-responding CD8+ T-cells were specific to NS4B in the donor vaccinated 30 years ago (P30), and up to 60% in the first time vaccinee (M1) (Figure 4A).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of NS4B-specific fraction shown in Figure 4A.

claim: At the peak of the response, up to 60% of all YF-responding CD8+ T-cells were specific to NS4B in donor M1.
source: At the peak of the response, approximately 24% of all YF-responding CD8+ T-cells were specific to NS4B in the donor vaccinated 30 years ago (P30), and up to 60% in the first time vaccinee (M1) (Figure 4A).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of NS4B-specific fraction shown in Figure 4A.

claim: NS4B-specific clonotypes could not be distinguished from other YF-responding clonotypes from their time traces alone, as they both responded with similar dynamics.
source: However, NS4B-specific clonotypes could not be distinguished from other YF-responding clonotypes from their time traces alone, as they both responded with similar dynamics (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Comparison of temporal dynamics shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: NS4B-specific TCR alpha repertoire shows biased V-usage and complementarity determining region 3 (CDR3) lengths.
source: The TCR alpha repertoire shows biased V-usage and complementarity determining region 3 (CDR3) lengths (Figure 4D).
evidence: Analysis of V-gene usage and CDR3 length distributions shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Beta chains of NS4B-specific TCRs formed several distinct clusters of highly similar sequences, with significant but less marked V-usage biases towards TRBV9, TRBV15, and TRBV6-1/2.
source: Beta chains formed several distinct clusters of highly similar sequences, with significant but less marked V-usage biases towards TRBV9, TRBV15, and TRBV6-1/2, as well as some bias in the length distribution (Figure 4E).
evidence: Analysis of TCR beta sequence similarity and V-gene usage shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Almost 37% of NS4B-specific clonotypes used TRBJ2-7.
source: Almost 37% of NS4B-specific clonotypes used TRBJ2-7.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of J-gene usage in NS4B-specific TCRs.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing and single-cell paired TCR sequencing collected data from 3500 cells corresponding to 164 clonotypes.
source: We collected data from 3500 cells corresponding to 164 clonotypes (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Quantitative description of single-cell sequencing data.

claim: Alpha-beta pairing in NS4B-specific TCRs seemed to be mostly random, with some exceptions.
source: Alpha-beta pairing seemed to be mostly random, with some exceptions: for instance, specific TCRs using the most dominant TRAV12-2 alpha motif were paired with many different beta chains with a broad usage of V-segments (Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A), but with a restricted CDR3β length of 13–14 amino acids.
evidence: Analysis of alpha-beta pairing patterns shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: TCRs using the most dominant TRAV12-2 alpha motif were paired with many different beta chains with a broad usage of V-segments, but with a restricted CDR3β length of 13–14 amino acids.
source: Alpha-beta pairing seemed to be mostly random, with some exceptions: for instance, specific TCRs using the most dominant TRAV12-2 alpha motif were paired with many different beta chains with a broad usage of V-segments (Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A), but with a restricted CDR3β length of 13–14 amino acids.
evidence: Analysis of pairing patterns for TRAV12-2 TCRs shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: TCRs using TRAV27 and TRBV9 segments were preferentially paired with one another.
source: TCRs using TRAV27 and TRBV9 segments were also preferentially paired with one another (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Analysis of pairing patterns shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Clustering of paired sequences using the TCRdist measure resulted in two large clusters corresponding to two major motifs with conserved V-usage.
source: Clustering of paired sequences using the TCRdist measure (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B) resulted in two large clusters corresponding to these two major motifs with conserved V-usage.
evidence: Clustering analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The preferential usage of the TRAV12 family was reported before for TCRs responsive to the NS4B epitope.
source: The preferential usage of the TRAV12 family was reported before for TCRs responsive to the NS4B epitope (Bovay et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: Citations to previous studies by Bovay et al., 2018 and Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: It was speculated that the CDR1α of the TRAV12 V-segment forms contacts with the peptide.
source: It was speculated (Bovay et al., 2018), that the CDR1α of this V-segment forms contacts with the peptide.
evidence: Citation to speculation in previous study by Bovay et al., 2018.

claim: Models of TCR-pMHC complexes showed that the TRAV12-2 TCRs formed more contacts with the peptide using CDR1α loops, and fewer contacts with CDR3α loops, in comparison to TRAV27 TCRs.
source: Models of TCR-pMHC complexes showed that the TRAV12-2 TCRs formed more contacts with the peptide using CDR1α loops, and fewer contacts with CDR3α loops, in comparison to TRAV27 TCRs (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Results from structural modeling and docking simulations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4A.

claim: CDR3α sequences of TRAV12-2 TCRs were very similar to the ones observed in the repertoire of the same donor prior to the immunization.
source: Interestingly, CDR3α sequences of TRAV12-2 TCRs were very similar to the ones observed in the repertoire of the same donor prior to the immunization, suggesting absence of epitope-driven selection of the CDR3α of these TCRs (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Comparison of CDR3α sequences shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4B.

claim: TCRs using TRAV12 and TRAV27 motifs represent two independent and distinct solutions to the binding of the NS4B epitope.
source: Based on these results, we hypothesize that TCRs using TRAV12 and TRAV27 motifs represent two independent and distinct solutions to the binding of the NS4B epitope.
evidence: Hypothesis based on structural modeling and sequence analysis results.

claim: Almost all NS4B-specific clonotypes 18 months after vaccination belonged to the conventional EMRA subset.
source: While almost all NS4B-specific clonotypes 18 months after vaccination belonged to the conventional EMRA subset, scRNAseq revealed huge heterogeneity of gene expression inside this population.
evidence: Analysis of memory subset distribution and gene expression from scRNAseq data.

claim: scRNAseq revealed huge heterogeneity of gene expression inside the EMRA population of NS4B-specific cells.
source: While almost all NS4B-specific clonotypes 18 months after vaccination belonged to the conventional EMRA subset, scRNAseq revealed huge heterogeneity of gene expression inside this population.
evidence: Analysis of gene expression heterogeneity from scRNAseq data.

claim: Unsupervised clustering by Seurat 3.0 software revealed three sub-phenotypes of NS4B-specific cells.
source: Unsupervised clustering by Seurat 3.0 software (Stuart et al., 2019; Butler et al., 2018) (see Materials and methods) revealed three sub-phenotypes of NS4B-specific cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: Clustering analysis of scRNAseq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 166 genes were differentially expressed according to the MAST algorithm between the three clusters of NS4B-specific cells.
source: Overall we found 166 genes that were differentially expressed according to the MAST algorithm (Finak et al., 2015) between these clusters (Figure 5B).
evidence: Differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Cells from cluster one showed high expression of cytotoxicity related genes GZMB, GNLY, GZMH, NKG7, PRF1, CX3CR1, SPON2, KLRD1, Hobit and T-bet transcription factors.
source: Cells from cluster one showed high expression of cytotoxicity related genes GZMB, GNLY, GZMH, NKG7, PRF1, CX3CR1, SPON2, KLRD1, Hobit and T-bet transcription factors (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Gene expression analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The combination of genes expressed in cluster one suggests that cytotoxicity is mediated by the perforin pathway.
source: The combination of these genes also suggests that this cytotoxicity is mediated by the perforin pathway.
evidence: Inference based on gene expression patterns in cluster one.

claim: The second cluster of cells is enriched in genes such as CCR7, TCF7, SELL, JUNB, LEF1, and especially IL7R which are essential for long-term survival and maintenance of memory T-cells.
source: The second cluster of cells is enriched in genes such as CCR7, TCF7, SELL, JUNB, LEF1, and especially IL7R which are essential for long-term survival and maintenance of memory T-cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B; Jeannet et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2010; Kaech et al., 2003; Jung et al., 2016; Schluns et al., 2000).
evidence: Gene expression analysis with citations to previous studies on memory T-cell biology.

claim: Cells in cluster 2 also express unique markers related to cytotoxicity: GZMK, LTB as well as KLRG1, KLRB1, T-bet, and GZMH, albeit at lower levels than cells in cluster 1.
source: However, these cells also express unique markers related to cytotoxicity: GZMK, LTB as well as KLRG1, KLRB1, T-bet, and GZMH, albeit at lower levels than cells in cluster 1.
evidence: Gene expression analysis comparing clusters 1 and 2.

claim: Very similar clusters of genes were found in single-cell RNAseq analysis of CD4-cytotoxic lymphocytes EMRA cells.
source: Very similar clusters of genes were found in single-cell RNAseq analysis of CD4-cytotoxic lymphocytes EMRA cells (Patil et al., 2018).
evidence: Citation to previous study by Patil et al., 2018.

claim: Cells in cluster two may be the precursors of cells in cluster 1.
source: The expression pattern of granzymes and killer-like receptors in our clusters suggests that cells in cluster two may be the precursors of cells in cluster 1.
evidence: Inference based on gene expression patterns and known biology of memory T-cell differentiation.

claim: The expression of GZMK (enriched in cluster 2) was shown to be prevalent in early memory stages.
source: The expression of GZMK (enriched in cluster 2) was shown to be prevalent in early memory stages (Harari et al., 2009; Bratke et al., 2005), while high levels of GZMB, GZMH, KLRB1, KLRG1, and ADGRG1 (enriched in cluster 1) are associated with more terminally differentiated memory cells with higher cytotoxic potential (Truong et al., 2019; Takata and Takiguchi, 2006).
evidence: Citations to previous studies on granzyme expression in memory T-cells.

claim: High levels of GZMB, GZMH, KLRB1, KLRG1, and ADGRG1 (enriched in cluster 1) are associated with more terminally differentiated memory cells with higher cytotoxic potential.
source: The expression of GZMK (enriched in cluster 2) was shown to be prevalent in early memory stages (Harari et al., 2009; Bratke et al., 2005), while high levels of GZMB, GZMH, KLRB1, KLRG1, and ADGRG1 (enriched in cluster 1) are associated with more terminally differentiated memory cells with higher cytotoxic potential (Truong et al., 2019; Takata and Takiguchi, 2006).
evidence: Citations to previous studies on markers of terminally differentiated memory T-cells.

claim: Cluster two has higher expression of genes encoding ribosomal proteins, which were recently reported to be a feature of memory precursor cells.
source: Interestingly, cluster two has higher expression of genes encoding ribosomal proteins, which were recently reported to be a feature of memory precursor cells (Araki et al., 2017).
evidence: Gene expression analysis with citation to previous study by Araki et al., 2017.

claim: The transition of cells between the two clusters is supported by the existence of cluster 3, which shows intermediate gene expression of cluster 1 and 2 markers.
source: The transition of cells between the two clusters is also supported by the existence of cluster 3, which shows intermediate gene expression of cluster 1 and 2 markers, and thus may represent cells gradually changing phenotype.
evidence: Analysis of gene expression patterns in cluster 3.

claim: Averaging mRNA counts over all cells of the same clonotype and repeating differential gene expression analysis obtained two clusters of clonotypes with the same enriched genes as observed for clusters of single cells.
source: To match single-cell gene expression data with measurements of clonotype concentrations obtained with TCRseq, we averaged mRNA counts over the all cells of the same clonotype, and repeated the differential gene expression analysis (see Materials and methods). We obtained two clusters of clonotypes with the same enriched genes (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A) as observed for clusters of single cells (Figure 5B), confirming the association of phenotype and clonotype.
evidence: Differential gene expression analysis of clonotype-averaged data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Clonotypes from both clusters expanded following the second immunization, indicating that both phenotypes are capable of response.
source: Clonotypes from both clusters expanded following the second immunization, indicating that both phenotypes are capable of response.
evidence: Analysis of clonotype expansion patterns after booster immunization.

claim: Clonotypes associated to cluster one had larger frequencies both on day 45 after the first vaccination and 18 months later before the booster shot, than clonotypes associated to cluster 2.
source: Clonotypes associated to cluster one had larger frequencies both on day 45 after the first vaccination (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, left), and 18 months later before the booster shot (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, right), than clonotypes associated to cluster 2.
evidence: Quantitative comparison of clonotype frequencies shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Even for T-cells recognizing the same epitope, particular clones are linked to particular memory phenotype.
source: This result suggests that even for T-cells recognizing the same epitope, particular clones are linked to particular memory phenotype.
evidence: Inference based on association between clonotypes and phenotypic clusters.

claim: Yellow fever vaccine is a live attenuated virus with a peak of viremia happening around day 7 after vaccine administration.
source: Yellow fever vaccine is a live attenuated virus with a peak of viremia happening around day 7 after vaccine administration (Miller et al., 2008; Akondy et al., 2009).
evidence: Citation to previous studies by Miller et al., 2008 and Akondy et al., 2009.

claim: Primary T-cell response sharply peaks around 2 weeks after YFV17D vaccination.
source: Primary T-cell response sharply peaks around 2 weeks after YFV17D (vaccine strain of yellow fever virus) vaccination (Miller et al., 2008; Akondy et al., 2009; Kohler et al., 2012; Pogorelyy et al., 2018; James et al., 2013).
evidence: Citations to multiple previous studies on YF vaccine response kinetics.

claim: The immune response to YF vaccine is very diverse and targets multiple epitopes inside the YF virus.
source: The immune response is very diverse and targets multiple epitopes inside the YF virus (de Melo et al., 2013; Co et al., 2002; Akondy et al., 2009; James et al., 2013; Blom et al., 2013).
evidence: Citations to multiple previous studies on YF vaccine epitope diversity.

claim: YF-specific T-cells could be found in the blood of vaccinated individuals years after vaccination.
source: Although most of the effector cells die shortly after viral clearance, YF-specific T-cells could be found in the blood of vaccinated individuals years (Akondy et al., 2009; Kongsgaard et al., 2017; James et al., 2013) and even decades after vaccination (Fuertes Marraco et al., 2015; Wieten et al., 2016).
evidence: Citations to previous studies on long-term YF-specific T-cell memory.

claim: Both T-cell activation marker staining and multimer staining show that the secondary response is much weaker than the primary one.
source: Both T-cell activation marker staining and multimer staining show that the secondary response is much weaker than the primary one (Kongsgaard et al., 2017), but their precise dynamics, diversity, and clonal structure are still unknown.
evidence: Citation to previous study by Kongsgaard et al., 2017.

claim: The precise dynamics, diversity, and clonal structure of the secondary response to YF vaccine are still unknown.
source: Both T-cell activation marker staining and multimer staining show that the secondary response is much weaker than the primary one (Kongsgaard et al., 2017), but their precise dynamics, diversity, and clonal structure are still unknown.
evidence: Statement about gaps in knowledge regarding secondary YF vaccine response.

claim: TCR repertoire sequencing allows for longitudinally tracking individual clones of responding T-cells irrespective of their epitope specificity.
source: TCR repertoire sequencing allows for longitudinally tracking individual clones of responding T-cells irrespective of their epitope specificity.
evidence: Description of TCR sequencing methodology and its capabilities.

claim: Single-cell RNAseq enables simultaneous quantification of thousands of transcripts per cell for thousands of cells, providing an unbiased characterization of immune cell phenotype.
source: Single-cell RNAseq (scRNAseq) enables simultaneous quantification of thousands of transcripts per cell for thousands of cells, providing an unbiased characterization of immune cell phenotype.
evidence: Description of scRNAseq methodology and its capabilities.

claim: Single-cell TCR sequencing produces paired αβ repertoire data, and thus could help discover conserved sequence motifs in one or both TCR chains.
source: Single-cell TCR sequencing produces paired αβ repertoire data, and thus could help discover conserved sequence motifs in one or both TCR chains.
evidence: Description of scTCRseq methodology and its capabilities.

claim: Conserved sequence motifs in TCRs encode TCR structural features essential to antigen recognition.
source: These motifs encode TCR structural features essential to antigen recognition (Dash et al., 2017; Glanville et al., 2017).
evidence: Citations to previous studies by Dash et al., 2017 and Glanville et al., 2017.

claim: Information about complete TCR sequences allows homological modeling of TCR structure.
source: Information about complete TCR sequences allows homological modeling of TCR structure (Schritt et al., 2019), which can be used for binding prediction with protein-protein docking (Pierce and Weng, 2013).
evidence: Citations to previous studies on TCR structural modeling and docking.

claim: Out of 62 NS4B-specific clonotypes sampled in the 10x Genomics experiment, 41 correct pairs were identified from bulk TCRseq data using the computational pairing algorithm.
source: Out of the 62 NS4B-specific clonotypes sampled in the 10x Genomics experiment, we were able to computationally identify 41 correct pairs from the bulk TCRseq data.
evidence: Validation of computational pairing method using single-cell data as ground truth.

claim: Out of 26 CD3+ T-cell clonotypes sampled in the 10x Genomics experiment, 20 were paired correctly using the computational pairing algorithm.
source: Out of 26 CD3+ T-cell clonotypes, 20 were paired correctly.
evidence: Validation of computational pairing method using single-cell data as ground truth.

claim: A clonotype with FDR adjusted p-value <0.01 (exact qCML-based test) was considered YF-responding if its log2-fold change estimate log2FC > 5 between any pairs of timepoints from 0 to the peak of the primary response (day 15).
source: A clonotype with FDR adjusted p-value <0.01 (exact qCML-based test) was considered YF-responding if its log2-fold change estimate log2FC > 5 between any pairs of timepoints from 0 to the peak of the primary response (day 15).
evidence: Description of statistical criteria for identifying YF-responding clonotypes.

claim: The usage of log2FC >5 threshold in addition to p-value threshold is important to filter statistically significant but small clonal expansions, which were previously shown to occur in healthy donors in the absence of vaccination on the timescale of one week.
source: The usage of log2FC >5 threshold in addition to p-value threshold is important to filter statistically significant but small clonal expansions, which were previously shown to occur in healthy donors in the absense of vaccination on the timescale of one week, see Pogorelyy et al. (2018).
evidence: Justification for threshold choice with citation to previous study.

claim: Over 98% of clonotypes were found exclusively in CD4 or CD8 compartment.
source: Over 98% of clonotypes were found exclusively in CD4 or CD8 compartment.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of CD4/CD8 phenotyping from TCR sequencing data.

claim: A small group of clonotypes (1.4% for TCR alpha and 0.14% for TCR beta for day 15 timepoint of donor M1) was present in both CD4 and CD8 compartments in comparable frequencies.
source: However, a small group of clonotypes (1.4% for TCR alpha and 0.14% for TCR beta for day 15 timepoint of donor M1) was present in both compartments in comparable frequencies.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of clonotypes present in both compartments.

claim: 152 TCRs passed the modeling step for TCR-pMHC complex modeling.
source: 152 TCRs passed the modeling step.
evidence: Quantitative description of structural modeling results.

claim: For each TCR, 1000 decoys were obtained in docking simulations.
source: For each TCR we obtained 1000 decoys in docking simulations.
evidence: Description of docking simulation methodology.

claim: The thirty best decoys (by interface score) were used to calculate a contact map with the bio3d R package.
source: The thirty best decoys (by interface score) were used to calculate a contact map with the bio3d R package (Grant et al., 2006).
evidence: Description of contact map calculation methodology with citation.

claim: Some docking decoys exhibit binding modes which are not found in natural TCRs.
source: It was previously shown (Pierce and Weng, 2013), that some docking decoys exhibit binding modes which are not found in natural TCRs.
evidence: Citation to previous study on docking artifacts.

claim: Vaccination with YFV17D leads to the recruitment of a diverse repertoire of T-cells, which is then available as immune memory for the secondary response years after the immunization.
source: To summarize, we show that vaccination with YFV17D leads to the recruitment of a diverse repertoire of T-cells, which is then available as immune memory for the secondary response years after the immunization.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on all experimental results.

claim: Even T-cells with the same epitope specificity show several distinct motifs in TCR and have different memory phenotypes.
source: Even T-cells with the same epitope specificity show several distinct motifs in TCR and have different memory phenotypes.
evidence: Summary of findings on TCR motifs and phenotypic heterogeneity.

claim: Heterogeneity of cells might be crucial for individual immune response robustness, underlying cross-reactive responses to similar viruses, and the possibility to escape mutants.
source: Such heterogeneity of cells might be crucial for individual immune response robustness, underlying cross-reactive responses to similar viruses, and the possibility to escape mutants, which could be tested directly in future studies.
evidence: Speculation about functional significance of observed heterogeneity.

claim: The diverse T-cell response is strongly focused on single HLA-A02 restricted epitope.
source: However, this diverse T-cell response is strongly focused on single HLA-A02 restricted epitope.
evidence: Summary of findings on immunodominance of NS4B epitope.

claim: Preexisting anti-YF immunity does not affect the formation of neutralizing antibodies to novel viruses in YF backbone chimeric vaccines.
source: It was shown that preexisting anti-YF immunity (Monath et al., 2002) does not affect the formation of neutralizing antibodies to the novel virus.
evidence: Citation to previous study by Monath et al., 2002.

claim: The virus is undetectable in the peripheral blood after booster vaccination.
source: It was shown that the virus is undetectable in the peripheral blood after booster vaccination (Reinhardt et al., 1998), meaning that the amount of available antigen is much lower, and so is the number of encounters and responding clonotypes.
evidence: Citation to previous study by Reinhardt et al., 1998 with inference about antigen availability.

claim: The transition between EM and EMRA phenotypes in CD8+ clones responding to yellow fever vaccine was previously measured using flow cytometry.
source: The transition between EM and EMRA phenotypes in CD8+ clones responding to yellow fever vaccine was previously measured using flow cytometry (Wieten et al., 2016; Fuertes Marraco et al., 2015).
evidence: Citations to previous studies on memory phenotype transitions.

claim: Several studies reported high precursor frequency of T-cells reactive to the NS4B epitope.
source: Several studies reported high precursor frequency of T-cells reactive to this epitope (Zhang et al., 2018; Bovay et al., 2018).
evidence: Citations to previous studies on NS4B-specific T-cell precursor frequency.

claim: Bovay et al. recently suggested that recognition of antigenic peptide through the germline-encoded CDR1 loop of the TRAV12 segment is one of the main reasons for high precursor frequency.
source: Bovay et al. (2018) recently suggested that recognition of antigenic peptide through the germline-encoded CDR1 loop of the TRAV12 segment is one of the main reasons for high precursor frequency.
evidence: Citation to hypothesis from previous study by Bovay et al., 2018.

claim: The hypothesis that recognition through CDR1 of TRAV12 explains high precursor frequency is supported by TCR structural modeling and TCR-pMHC docking simulations, as well as by the analysis of the NS4B-specific T-cell repertoire.
source: This hypothesis is supported by our TCR structural modeling and TCR-pMHC docking simulations, as well as by the analysis of the NS4B-specific T-cell repertoire.
evidence: Summary of evidence supporting hypothesis from structural and sequence analysis.

claim: The magnitude of CD8 response depends on the viral load.
source: It was previously shown that the magnitude CD8 response depends on the viral load (Akondy et al., 2015).
evidence: Citation to previous study by Akondy et al., 2015.

claim: According to the programmed proliferation hypothesis, a single encounter of a TCR with an antigen triggers several rounds of T-cell division.
source: This may be indirect evidence for the programmed proliferation hypothesis (Moore et al., 2019) according to which a single encounter of a TCR with an antigen triggers several rounds of T-cell division.
evidence: Citation to hypothesis from previous study by Moore et al., 2019.
